title: The Man Born Blind Receives His Sight
summary: Jesus heals a man blind from birth by putting mud on his eyes and sending him to wash in the Pool of Siloam. Because it is the Sabbath, the Pharisees interrogate the man and his frightened parents, and when the man insists that Jesus must be from God, they throw him out. Jesus finds him, the man believes and worships, and Jesus declares that he came so the blind may see and those who claim to see may become blind.
story: Jesus has just said, “I am the light of the world” (8:12), and in 9:5 he says it again before showing what it means. The chapter stands as a picture of the whole Gospel in miniature. A man who has never seen moves step by step toward faith, calling Jesus a man, then a prophet, then one from God, and finally Lord, whom he worships. Meanwhile the religious authorities, who are sure they see, move step by step into deeper blindness. It also shows the cost of confessing Jesus, as the man loses his place in the synagogue, which prepares for Jesus' teaching about the good shepherd in chapter 10.
historical:
The Pool of Siloam lay at the southern end of the old city of David in Jerusalem, fed by water from the Gihon spring through the tunnel cut in King Hezekiah's day (2 Kings 20:20). In 2004 workers repairing a sewer uncovered the steps of a large pool from the Second Temple period at this site, which most archaeologists identify with the pool of Jesus' time. As with Bethesda in chapter 5, John's knowledge of Jerusalem's geography has been confirmed by digging. The pool was also connected with the Feast of Tabernacles, since the water poured at the altar during the feast was drawn from Siloam.

Verse 22 says the Jews had agreed that anyone confessing Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue. The Jews here must be the authorities, since the parents who fear them are Jews too. Scholars debate how this fits history. J. Louis Martyn argued that John was reading back a later situation, linking it to a synagogue prayer against heretics that some date to the late first century. Many scholars now doubt that link, noting that the prayer's date, wording, and target are uncertain and that local exclusions could have happened at many times, including during Jesus' ministry. Either way, the chapter reflects a real and painful separation, and it describes the leaders' action, not the character of the Jewish people. Reading it as the latter has fed Christian hostility toward Jews for centuries, and the text itself doesn't support it.
cultural:
Many in the ancient world assumed that disability was punishment for sin. The disciples' question reflects a debate: if the man was born blind, had he sinned in the womb, or were his parents to blame? The Old Testament speaks of consequences reaching to children (Exodus 20:5), but it also rejects the idea that children bear their parents' guilt (Ezekiel 18:20), and the book of Job argues at length against the claim that suffering always reveals sin. A man blind from birth had no way to earn a living except begging, often near the temple or city gates.

Saliva was thought in the ancient world to have healing properties, and Jesus uses it elsewhere (Mark 7:33; 8:23). Making mud, however, involved kneading, which the Mishnah lists among the thirty-nine kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath, so the healing was a deliberate provocation. When the authorities tell the man, “Give glory to God!” (9:24), they are using a formula that called a person to tell the truth under oath, as Joshua said to Achan (Joshua 7:19). Being put out of the synagogue meant losing one's standing in the community: its worship, its fellowship, and often its practical support.
literary: The chapter is one of John's finest pieces of drama, built in scenes like a play: the healing (9:1-7), the neighbors (9:8-12), the first interrogation (9:13-17), the parents (9:18-23), the second interrogation (9:24-34), and Jesus with the man and then with the Pharisees (9:35-41). Jesus is present only at the beginning and end; in between, the man stands alone. The irony is thick. The man who was blind grows in sight and in courage, answering his judges with wit, while the experts repeat “we know” and understand nothing. The verb to see and the word blind recur throughout, so that by the last verses physical sight has become a picture of spiritual sight. John notes that Siloam means “Sent,” a quiet pointer to Jesus, the one sent by the Father.

outline.t: Jesus heals a man born blind
The Pharisees question him: a prophet
The second interrogation and the man thrown out
Jesus finds him; sight and blindness

doctrines.note: Jesus refuses the disciples' assumption that this suffering must be traced to a particular sin (9:3). He turns the question from why to what God will do. The chapter doesn't explain all suffering, but it closes off the easy link between a person's pain and their guilt.

Faith grows through the chapter as testimony under pressure. The man begins with what he knows, “I was blind, but now I see” (9:25), and comes to full confession only when Jesus reveals himself: “Lord, I believe” (9:38).

Jesus says, “For judgment I have come into this world” (9:39). His coming exposes people. Those who admit their blindness receive sight, while those who claim to see without him are confirmed in their blindness (9:41).

words.note: Tuphlos, blind. It occurs thirteen times in the chapter. It begins as a physical description and ends as a spiritual diagnosis when the Pharisees ask, “Are we blind too?” (9:40). Isaiah had spoken of the Lord's servant opening blind eyes (Isaiah 42:7), which gives the healing a messianic weight.

Aposunagōgos, put out of the synagogue. The word appears only in John (9:22; 12:42; 16:2) and nowhere earlier in Greek literature that survives. It names exclusion from the local Jewish community, the price the man pays for his testimony, and Jesus warns his disciples of the same in 16:2.

Proskuneō, to worship, originally to bow down before someone. It can mean respectful homage, but in John it is used for the worship of God (4:20-24). The man's worship of Jesus in 9:38 is the climax of his growing sight.

Silōam, the pool of Siloam, from a Hebrew word connected with sending. John translates it as “Sent” (9:7), linking the water that heals to Jesus, whom the Gospel repeatedly calls the one sent by the Father.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus as the light of the world in action. The prophets promised that in the day of God's salvation the eyes of the blind would be opened (Isaiah 35:5; 42:7), and the man himself says no one had ever heard of such a thing (9:32). The healing is a sign that the new creation has begun: Jesus uses mud from the ground, recalling God forming the first man from dust, and gives sight to one who never had it. The chapter also shows Jesus as the shepherd who seeks out the one thrown out. When the man is expelled, Jesus finds him (9:35). He reveals himself as the Son of Man, the heavenly figure of Daniel 7, and receives the man's worship.

hard.q: Was the man born blind just so that God could display his power in him?
hard.a:
Read quickly, 9:3 can sound as if God made the man suffer for decades as a stage for a miracle. Interpreters answer in several ways. Some note that the Greek can be punctuated differently, so that Jesus' sentence ends with “neither this man nor his parents sinned,” and the purpose clause joins the following verse: so that the works of God may be displayed, we must work while it is day. On that reading Jesus is not explaining why the blindness happened but saying what he will do about it. Others keep the traditional punctuation and read it as a statement of God's purpose that sees suffering within his larger work without claiming he inflicted it for show. Still others emphasize that Jesus is primarily rejecting the disciples' theory of sin and blame rather than offering a full account of why suffering exists.

All these readings agree that Jesus refuses to treat suffering as a puzzle about guilt, and that his response to it is to act. The Bible as a whole doesn't give a complete answer to why God allows suffering; it shows a God who enters it and a Savior who heals.

questions: The man could say only what he knew: “I was blind, but now I see.” How might your own honest testimony matter even when you can't answer every question?
His parents were afraid to speak because of what it might cost them. Where does fear of losing your place keep you quiet?
Jesus says those who claim to see remain guilty. What makes it hard to admit our own blindness?
